Title: Invisible to Humans, Triggered by Agents: Stealthy Jailbreak Attacks on Mobile Vision–Language Agents
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous mobile agents that execute tasks through GUI interaction. However, their security under realistic deployment constraints remains insufficiently understood. Existing attacks typically rely on persistent visual manipulations, privileged system access, or iterative jailbreak interactions, limiting their practicality. In this work, we identify a previously overlooked discrepancy between human and agent interactions: automated mobile agents generate near-zero touchcontact signals that systematically differ from human touches. Based on this observation, we introduce agent-only perceptual injection, a new attack paradigm that exposes malicious prompts only during agent interactions while keeping them unexposed during normal user operation. To realize this attack, we propose a low-privilege framework that combines in-app prompt embedding, interaction-triggered activation, and HG-IDA*, an efficient one-shot jailbreak optimization method tailored to mobile UI constraints. Experiments on multiple Android applications and LVLM backends, such as GPT-4o, show that our attacks reliably hijack both agent planning and execution. Our method achieves up to 95.0% planning attack success rate and 82.5% execution attack success rate on commercial LVLM backends. These findings reveal a new interaction-level attack surface and highlight the need for provenance-aware defenses in mobile agent systems.
Major_Contribution_Result: The paper identifies agent-only perceptual injection for mobile vision–language agents: malicious prompts are exposed during low-contact agent GUI interaction but kept unexposed under normal human touch. The authors propose a low-privilege in-app framework combining activation and detoxification mechanisms and evaluate 40 curated injection instances. They report substantial end-to-end success on several backends, including GPT-4o at 82.5% plan-level (Tasr) and 75.0% execution-level (Rasr) success, and Gemini-2.0 at 95.0% Tasr and 82.5% Rasr.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: The authors state the study focuses on prompt-injection attacks embedded in Android apps under a controlled mobile-agent environment, without exhaustive robustness testing across broader devices, alternative agent architectures, or future OS UI changes. The attack assumes an adversary can modify and redistribute an application, which is realistic for third-party ecosystems but not all distribution channels. Detoxification search is performed on short, screen-bounded prompts and may need adaptation for longer or multimodal payloads.
Critics: This is an attack/red-teaming paper on multimodal mobile agents with perception-chain injections, not a defense or release-gate evaluation framework. Reported Tasr/Rasr numbers are for the authors' curated 40-instance setting and named backends, so they should not be generalized as universal mobile-agent ASR. It expands LLM-agent security evaluation into GUI/perception provenance, but does not provide post-mitigation reassessment or cross-platform agent benchmarks beyond the studied Android setup.
